public_rationale: The TechCrunch story Marcus cites exists. It is by Connie Loizos and was published on 9 February 2026 (e1). It describes in-progress UC Berkeley research at a 200-person tech company. In that research, an engineer said that with AI 'you don't work less. You just work the same amount or even more' (e1). The story also quotes a Hacker News commenter who said stress had tripled while productivity rose 'maybe 10%' (e2). The researchers link the extra work to 'fatigue, burnout' (e3). This meets the claim that some coders are starting to report burnout with modest gains. One caveat: the researchers say AI's boost to what workers can do is real (e3). The 'modest gains' part therefore rests mainly on the forum comment.
limitations: The evidence is a small set of reports: one interviewed engineer and one anonymous forum commenter. It does not show how common burnout is among coders.
The Berkeley study covers tech workers at one company, not only programmers, and the story does not quantify their gains.
The METR item on coding speed (e4) is dated after the post and serves only as context for 'wicked fast'.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLMs write code very fast, but some coders report burnout and only modest gains compared with that burnout.

our_interpretation: The claim is about reports, not a population rate. It holds if credible recent reporting, especially the cited TechCrunch story, documents some coders or engineers describing burnout alongside modest gains.
'Wicked fast' is uncontroversial framing and is treated as secondary.
criteria.support_condition: The TechCrunch story by Connie Loizos, or similar reporting from the period, documents engineers or coders using AI who report burnout and gains that are modest compared with the extra strain.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The TechCrunch story does not exist or does not describe burnout among AI-using coders, and no other reporting from the period shows it.

evidence.excerpt: As one engineer told them, “You had thought that maybe, oh, because you could be more productive with AI, then you save some time, you can work less. But then really, you don’t work less. You just work the same amount or even more.”
evidence.explanation: The Loizos story exists and reports an engineer at an AI-embracing tech company describing more work, not less.

evidence.excerpt: expectations have tripled, stress has tripled and actual productivity has only gone up by maybe 10%.
evidence.explanation: The story quotes a tech worker reporting stress that has tripled against a gain of about 10%. That matches 'modest gains relative to that burnout'.

evidence.explanation: The underlying UC Berkeley/HBR research reports burnout among AI adopters. It also says the augmentation is real, which tempers the 'modest gains' part.
